asSun.p: Look at the horse on this card for a second. It's walking. Nobody's whipping it on, and everyone standing in front of it has to work out what they're going to do about that. Death is Scorpio's card, the way The Emperor is Aries's and Strength is Leo's, and that's why it comes to you with a Scorpio Sun. Scorpio is fixed water, and its old ruler is Mars, with Pluto added by modern astrologers. The Sun has no special standing in Scorpio. It isn't strengthened there and it isn't weakened either. It's a visitor in somebody else's house, and it picks up the manners of the host. So your sense of who you are has Mars in it, the fighter, only the fighting mostly happens out of sight. Fixed water doesn't rush about. It sits still on top and it's very hard to drain, and anyone who's tried to talk you out of something you'd set your mind on knows exactly what I mean.

You decide things once. It can take you a long time to get there, and the people around you often don't see the deciding happen, but when you're done you're done, and the old job or the old friend or the old way of doing Christmas just stops existing for you. Your mate spends six months complaining about a flatmate and you say, fairly flatly, 'so move'. At work there's a restructure coming and you've updated your CV a fortnight before the announcement, because you read the room months ago. In an argument you give up the small points quickly and don't move an inch on the one that matters, and the other person often works out which one it was on the drive home. You're private about what you want, too. You tell people after you've got it, sometimes years after.

You let people change. Because you've shed a few versions of yourself, you don't hold anyone to who they were at nineteen. A friend who got sober, a sister who used to be awful to you, a colleague who messed up badly last year, you deal with the person standing in front of you, and that's rarer than it sounds. There's a very practical side to the card in you as well. When someone dies, or a business folds, or a marriage ends, you're the one who can make the phone calls, find the paperwork, cancel the direct debits and tell the kids in plain words. Other people freeze at the admin of an ending. You get on with it, and it's a real kindness, even if from outside it looks a bit cold.

You keep things back as insurance. You tend to know more about everyone's situation than they know about yours, and part of you likes it that way, because it feels safe. You'll have an exit plan in a relationship that's going perfectly well, a savings account nobody else knows about, a version of events you haven't told your business partner yet. Mars rules the sign, and a Mars that can't fight in the open fights by holding cards. The cost is that the people close to you feel slightly audited. Your partner tells you about some small thing they got wrong, and they can see you file it away. After a few years of that, some people stop telling you things, and you might not notice when it started.

When something goes badly wrong, a Scorpio Sun takes charge of it. Lose a job and by dinner time you've told nobody and made a list of every recruiter you know. Find out a friend has been lying to you and you're perfectly pleasant at the next birthday, while working out exactly who else knew and for how long. Some days later the Mars side turns up. You cut someone off, often the wrong someone, or throw yourself at the gym or a spreadsheet at eleven at night. The people around you get a closed door and a polite voice, and they can't tell whether they're being blamed. It helps to tell someone the whole thing, including the bit you're ashamed of, and let them not fix it. Hard physical work helps too, digging out a garden bed or stripping paint off a door, anything that uses the anger up.

You pick people on purpose, and once you've picked, you're in with the whole of yourself. What surprises your partners is how badly you want to be known and how hard you make it. You'd like them to understand you without having to explain, and when they get it wrong it feels like a small betrayal, which is a lot to put on someone who forgot you can't stand coriander. Pride comes into it more than you'd admit. You're rarely the first to say sorry, and after a real row you'd sooner go without them for a week than be seen to come back first. The partners who last with you usually have a life of their own that you can't quite get to the bottom of, because you respect what you can't take over. When you want something from them, ask for it in so many words, even though it feels like giving ground.

At work you need real say over your own patch. The title matters to you less than whether anyone is checking over your shoulder, and you'll put up with low pay for a long while before you'll put up with being micromanaged. You're good at the jobs other people avoid. Investigations, the audit, the numbers that don't add up, the client who's about to walk. You like finding out what's really going on, and you're good at keeping it to yourself until the right moment. You're competitive in a quiet way, too. You don't need to be seen winning, you need to have won. The trouble is loyalty in both directions. You'll stay years for a boss who backed you once, and never quite forgive one who didn't. Every so often check whether you're still in a job because it suits you or because leaving would feel like losing.

At twenty a Scorpio Sun is usually all or nothing about everything. You fall for people completely, you hold grudges completely, and you cut friends out with a thoroughness that frightens your mother a bit. By the mid-thirties most have been through at least one real ending, a divorce, a death, a career that collapsed, and come out the other side, and it changes them. The intensity is still there, it's just got better aim. You stop picking fights to find out who's on your side, and you start asking. The fifties often bring a kind of authority people don't argue with, and younger colleagues and relatives bring you their worst news first. The thing to watch then is the old grudges, which a fixed sign can carry for decades without noticing the weight.

Next time you're partway through deciding something that affects someone close to you, the job, the move, whether to keep seeing a friend, tell them before you've finished. One sentence, 'I'm thinking about this', with no reasons and no plan attached. It'll feel exposed, as if you've given something away for nothing. Notice afterwards that the decision is still yours, and that they probably liked being told.

asMoon.p: Your Moon is in Scorpio, and Death is Scorpio's card, so that's how this one reaches you. The Moon is in fall in Scorpio, which is the old term for a planet sitting in a sign that makes its job hard. The Moon's job is comfort, being soothed, feeling safe enough to let your guard down. Scorpio is fixed water ruled by Mars, and it doesn't trust easy comfort, so the Moon here has to go the long way round to get what it needs. Fixed means feelings don't pass through. They settle and stay. The Moon still gets fed, just indirectly, through closeness that's had years to prove itself, through privacy, through something being properly finished. On the card there's a small child in front of the horse, looking straight up at the rider without any fear at all. I'd say that child is nearer to how you feel inside than your face ever lets on.

Your feelings arrive quietly and then won't leave. Someone says something offhand at a family dinner and you're fine all evening, and at two in the morning you're lying awake replaying it word for word. A text from your ex's mum on your birthday can wreck a whole afternoon, and you won't mention it to anyone. When a friend cancels plans twice, you don't get cross. You make a small note somewhere inside and make slightly fewer plans with them afterwards. You need a lot of time alone with the door shut, and that's how you digest things, even if it looks like sulking to everyone else. Your moods sit in the body as well. Your stomach tightens before you know you're upset, and when something's wrong, sleep goes first and your appetite follows.

You remember the dates. When a friend's dad dies you're at the funeral like everyone else, but you're also the one who texts on his birthday the following year, and the year after that, when nobody else does. You know grief doesn't stop when the casseroles do. People tell you things they've never said out loud, because they can feel that you won't flinch and you won't pass it on, and they're right on both counts. A Scorpio Moon also has a very good ear for the gap between what someone says and how they feel. A teenager you're driving home says the party was fine and you know within a second it wasn't, and you know to wait until you're both looking at the road.

With the Moon in fall, comfort feels a bit suspicious to you. When someone's kind for no reason, part of you goes looking for the reason. You can be offered exactly the reassurance you wanted and not be able to take it in, because you've already decided it's just what people say. Jealousy lives near here too, and it's usually quiet. You won't make a scene about your partner's new colleague. You'll ask one extra question about her each week, casual as anything, and keep the answers. The other version is punishing yourself for needing anything at all. You'd sooner go without than ask and be let down, and then you're hurt that nobody noticed you went without. The people around you can't always tell what they did wrong, and often they didn't do anything.

Stress goes inward with a Scorpio Moon. Something awful happens, a diagnosis in the family, a betrayal, a redundancy, and your first move is to shut the door and go under with it. You don't ring anyone. You might clean the entire kitchen at midnight, or lie in the dark with your phone face down. People who love you get one-word answers. Days later, sometimes a fortnight, it comes up through the body, a jaw that aches, a stomach that won't settle, sleep that breaks at four every morning, or it comes out as one sharp remark to someone who didn't deserve it. Water helps, and I mean actual water. A long bath, a swim, a walk in the rain. It also helps to have a person you ring first, the same one every time, so you don't have to decide who's safe while you're in the middle of it.

What you need from a partner is to feel you've been let all the way in, and that they've let you in too. Half-closeness makes you anxious in a way you don't always recognise as anxiety. It comes out as small checks, the same question asked twice in a week, going cold to see if they follow. Cancer and Pisces share Scorpio's element, and people with those signs strong in their charts often feel easy to you straight away, because they don't need a feeling explained before they'll believe it. Touch matters a great deal to you, and being held for a long while after a hard day settles you in a way no talking does. The thing to tell a partner early on is that when you go quiet you aren't always angry. Sometimes you're just full, and you need them to stay in the room.

Your feelings need somewhere private to go during the working day, and open-plan offices are hard on you. You do your best with a door, or headphones, or long stretches on your own. A lot of Scorpio Moons end up working near the hard parts of life, nursing, counselling, a crisis line, a funeral home, anywhere people are frightened and something needs looking at properly. You're steady in those rooms. You also tend to feel a workplace going bad months before anyone says so, from who's stopped eating lunch together and who's started shutting their door. The cost of all that is that you take it home, and a Scorpio Moon doesn't put things down easily. Have something you do on the way back, the same walk, a particular album, ten minutes in the parked car, so the day doesn't follow you through the front door.

In your twenties a Scorpio Moon tends to feel everything at full volume and show almost none of it. You fall hard, you get hurt, you keep a very private list of who let you down, and you might not cry in front of anyone for years. The thirties are usually when something gets past the guard, a loss or a breakup, and you find out you can come apart in front of someone and still be loved the next morning. After that you choose people more carefully and you're kinder to your own moods. By the fifties a lot of Scorpio Moons have softened in ways that surprise their families. You cry at the football. You ring a sister for no reason. What needs looking after later on is your own grief, because you've been so good at everyone else's that nobody thinks to ask about yours.

When a feeling has been sitting in you for more than a day, write its name on a scrap of paper, one word, like 'jealous' or 'left out', and put it in your pocket. Carry it until you've said it to one person, in that same one word if you like. It doesn't need explaining. Then tear the paper up and put it in the bin.

asRising.p: Scorpio was coming up over the eastern horizon when you were born, so it sits on your first house, the house of the body and of how you walk into a room. Death belongs to Scorpio, which makes it the card strangers meet before they've met the rest of you. It also makes Mars the ruler of your whole chart, with Pluto as its modern co-ruler, so wherever Mars sits in your chart carries more weight than it would for most people. Fixed water on the Ascendant looks calm. A lot goes on underneath and very little of it reaches your face. In whole-sign houses the rest of the chart follows from that doorway. Taurus lands on your seventh house of partners, Leo on your tenth of career, and Aquarius on your fourth of home, and that Aquarius fourth is why a lot of Scorpio risings, so closed at the front door, keep a surprisingly open house, friends dropping in at odd hours and nobody asked to take their shoes off.

You notice exits. Walk into a party and you've clocked where the door is, who's annoyed with whom and who's had too much to drink before you've got your coat off. In a job interview you give careful, short answers and watch their faces, and they tend to come away unsure whether you liked them. A new neighbour stops you at the letterbox and walks off ten minutes later having told you their job, their divorce and why they moved, and realising they don't know your surname. People tell you you're hard to read and you're a bit pleased about it. You go still when you're paying attention, which is most of the time, and strangers sometimes take the stillness for disapproval. You rarely start anything loudly. You wait until you've got the measure of it and then move all at once, which throws people who'd decided you were shy.

Your instincts about people are usually right, and fast. You'll meet a new manager and know within one coffee whether they can be trusted, and it takes everyone else six months to catch up. That's the Mars ruler doing its job, scanning for threat, and it makes you good protection for the people you care about. Friends bring new partners round to meet you on purpose. The other gift, which nobody expects from someone who looks like you do, is a very dry sense of humour. You say one flat line at the worst moment of a bad meeting and the whole room breathes out. Because nobody saw it coming it lands twice as hard, and people remember you for it for years.

Being hard to read has a cost you don't always count. Because you never look flustered, people assume you're fine, and help doesn't get offered. Because you watch everything, you sometimes see a threat that isn't there, and treat a new colleague's friendliness as an angle before they've done a thing to earn it. You also hate being seen as a beginner. You'll skip the pottery class, or keep quiet in the language you're half learning, sooner than look clumsy in front of strangers. So a lot of good things never get started, simply because they'd have to be started in public. Some of that is pride and some of it is plain self-protection, and you usually know which.

When things go wrong, Scorpio rising shuts the face down first. You get stiller, quieter and very polite, and you start sorting the people around you into safe and not safe. In a tense work meeting you say almost nothing, and afterwards everyone wonders what you're planning. After a breakup you might delete the photos, buy a new coat and turn up on Monday looking completely unbothered. It catches up with you a few days on, usually in the shoulders, and in a sudden need to be entirely alone for a weekend. Colleagues read the calm as not caring, and a partner can feel shut out of a room they're standing in. A boxing class helps, or a hard run, anything that gives Mars, your chart ruler, something to hit. So does letting someone you trust see your face with the composure off.

With Scorpio rising, Taurus sits on your seventh house, the house of partners, and it's very common for you to end up with someone steady, sensual, a bit stubborn and not remotely mysterious. They don't play games, and at first that almost bores you. Later it's the thing you trust most about them. Early on you're hard to get to know. You'll let someone talk for three dates and give them very little back, and a lot of good people give up before the fourth. Venus rules Taurus, so what your seventh house wants is pleasure without strategy, dinner that's just dinner. So show interest before you're sure it's safe. Tell them you like them while it still feels like a risk.

Leo falls on your tenth house, career and reputation, and Leo squares Scorpio, two fixed signs that don't give an inch to each other, so there's friction built in. You come across as private and watchful, and yet the working life that suits you puts you in front of people anyway, leading, presenting, being the name on the report. A lot of Scorpio risings get handed authority before they've asked for it, simply because they look like they can handle it. You interview well if the panel likes quiet competence and badly if they want sparkle. You're good wherever you need to read people fast, sales, negotiation, policing, journalism, recruiting. What catches you out is recognition. The Leo tenth wants its credit and you're too guarded to ask for it, so say what you did, in the meeting, with your name attached.

Scorpio rising at twenty is mostly armour. Black clothes or the equivalent, a stare that keeps people back, a lot of watching at parties, and a real fear of being seen trying. People assume you're older and harder than you are. Through the thirties the face usually softens a little. You've been hurt, you've survived it, and you don't need the whole guard up for every stranger. This is often when the Leo tenth house starts to pay off, and people who used to find you intimidating start calling you impressive. By the fifties Scorpio rising tends to have real presence and far less need to defend it. You still see through people in about four seconds, and you're gentler about what you do with it. Left to itself, though, the self-containment can go too far, and there are Scorpio risings of seventy whose oldest friends couldn't tell you what frightens them.

At the next gathering where you hardly know anyone, choose one person and let them see you unsure of something within the first ten minutes. Ask what a word means, admit you've never been to this suburb before, say you're hopeless at these things. Keep it small and true. Then watch what they do. Most people move a little closer, and quite often they tell you something true back.

asBirthCard.p: This one doesn't come from any planet in your chart. It comes from your birthdate. Add up every digit, and if the total's over 22 add those digits together again, and a total of 13, 49 or 58 brings you to thirteen, which is Death. Thirteen is one more than twelve, and twelve is a complete set, twelve months, twelve signs, twelve houses. So thirteen is what comes after something has been completed. It sits straight after The Hanged Man, the card of hanging upside down and waiting, and just before Temperance, the card of mixing things back together slowly. Death is the moment in between, when the waiting stops and something actually goes. In the old Marseille decks the thirteenth card often had no name printed on it at all. In astrology the card belongs to Scorpio, but that's the card's own nature, and it says nothing about your signs.

Your life probably keeps changing shape, often on a schedule you didn't pick. You've moved house more than most. You look at photos from ten years ago and don't quite recognise the person, and it isn't only the haircut. There's a certain kind of conversation you seem to end up in a lot. A friend in a hospital corridor. A colleague telling you in the car park that their marriage is over. Someone at a wedding telling you about the brother who isn't there. You're also the one who clears out the house, whether it's your own after a breakup or a grandparent's after the funeral, and you're good at deciding what goes. The pattern asks very little of you in the quiet years. It's the turning points where it gets loud.

You can often feel that something's finished a while before anyone else will say so, a project, a band, a friendship that's been running on memory, and you can say it out loud without being cruel. Groups need someone who can do that, and they rarely thank them for it. At work you might be the one who shuts a product down properly, so the customers and the people who built it land somewhere decent. You're also good at the part after. The first week in a new city, the first job after a redundancy, the first Christmas after a divorce, you tend to know what to do with them, and you can make a strange flat feel like home within a month. Friends who are starting over usually end up ringing you, because you've done it so many times yourself.

You get used to endings, and then you start expecting them. In a good stretch, a steady job, a kind partner, a year with nothing going wrong, you can feel oddly restless, or catch yourself waiting for the floor to give way. Some people with this card leave first so it can't be done to them. They quit the job just before the review, or end things once the relationship gets comfortable, and call it knowing when something's over. Sometimes it is. Sometimes ordinary happiness just feels unfamiliar and they don't trust it. Before you pull the plug on anything, ask whether it has actually died or only gone quiet for a while.

Under real pressure this pattern gets decisive very fast. A loss hits, or a job goes, and within days you're changing things, the flat, the hair, the phone number, the diet, as if you could get the next chapter started before the grief catches up. For a week or so that works. Then it stops working. The grief usually arrives late, set off by something small, a song in a shop, and it undoes you in a way you didn't see coming. The people around you can find the speed of it hard to be near. They're still in shock and you've already packed a box. Slow the outside changes right down if you can, no big decisions for a couple of months, and let the sad part run at its own pace with someone nearby, even if all they do is sit with you on the back step.

Across a lifetime your relationships tend to come in distinct eras, and each one changes you enough that you're a slightly different person going into the next. That's no failing. Some people with this card stay with one partner for fifty years, and the pattern shows up as that one relationship ending and starting again several times inside itself, after a move, after children, after an illness, after the kids leave home. Either way, the partners who suit you are the ones who don't panic when you change. The ones who want you exactly as you were on the day you met tend to find you hard work. If you're in something long, say so out loud when you feel one of those turns coming, so the two of you go through it together.

Your working life probably won't run in one straight line, and trying to force it into one tends to make you miserable. People with this card often have two or three careers, and the jumps between them look sudden from outside, though they've been coming for a long time. You're useful anywhere something needs closing, clearing or starting again. Restructures, deceased estates, editing, demolition, the tail end of a project everyone else has lost interest in. Thirteen is also a card about what's left once the extra has gone, and you're good at cutting. The risk is cutting because you're bored, reorganising a team just because it's been stable for two years. Before you tear something down at work, check who else has to live in what's left.

The pattern usually feels like chaos in your twenties. Things end that you didn't want to end, a first love, a first job, a family home, and you take each one as a disaster. By the mid-thirties most people with this card can see the shape of it. They've had two or three complete changes of life, and they've noticed each one left them more like themselves, even the ones that hurt badly. They stop taking every ending as proof that something's wrong with them. The fifties often bring the endings that come to everyone around then, parents, bodies, careers winding down, and people with this card tend to meet those better than their friends do, because they've had the practice. The work later in life is letting some things stay, and finding out you can enjoy a long stretch where nothing changes much.

Once a season, go through one drawer, one folder on your computer or one list of contacts, and let go of three things that belong to a version of you that's finished. An old email address, a gym card, the notes from a course you're never going back to. Before you bin each one, say out loud what it was for. Keep it quick. Twenty minutes, then shut the drawer and go and make a cup of tea.
